story.title: Mass Protests Erupt in Madrid Over Housing Crisis Following Elderly Woman's Eviction
story.summary: Tens of thousands of people protested in Madrid against Spain's housing crisis after the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home of over 70 years. The incident has sparked widespread anger and calls for government action to address rising housing costs and prevent further evictions.

timeline_highlights.title: Protests Erupt in India Demanding Resignation of Election Chief
timeline_highlights.summary: A youth group known as the 'Cockroach' movement has threatened to resume mass protests unless Gyanesh Kumar resigns as head of India's election commission. This demand follows allegations of election rigging, which have also prompted opposition parties, including Congress, to join the protests. Police have responded with tear gas to disperse demonstrators.

explore_lenses.label: Why was Maricarmen evicted despite appeals?
explore_lenses.title: A court ruling ended a protected tenancy dispute
explore_lenses.summary: The eviction followed a long legal fight over succession to a rent-regulated tenancy, rather than an immediate removal without prior proceedings. Her vulnerability prompted appeals and protests, but did not stop enforcement after the owners prevailed in court.

claims.text: Maricarmen Abascal was removed on September 23, 2026, at the fourth attempted eviction from the Retiro flat where she had lived since 1956.

The owner, Urbagestión Desarrollo e Inversión S.L., argued that a second succession to the 1956 tenancy was invalid; Euronews reported that Spain's Supreme Court ruled for the owners in March 2026, overturning an earlier ruling for Abascal.
The UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights requested that Spain halt the eviction and ensure adequate housing, but that request did not prevent the removal.
Madrid City Council says it had offered Abascal housing options, while her lawyer said the company would not grant even a short delay to remove her belongings.

The UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights requested that Spain halt the eviction and ensure adequate housing, but that request did not prevent the removal.
Madrid City Council says it had offered Abascal housing options, while her lawyer said the company would not grant even a short delay to remove her belongings.
explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: The publicly consulted reporting does not specify the terms of the council's housing offers or why they did not produce a settled alternative before the eviction.

explore_lenses.label: Why has this case become a housing flashpoint?
explore_lenses.title: A personal eviction crystallized wider affordability fears
explore_lenses.summary: The case became a rallying point because it combined an elderly disabled tenant's removal with Madrid's broader affordability pressures and anger at property investment. It also exposed competing views of which level of government should have prevented the outcome.

claims.text: The Madrid Tenants' Union says the new owner raised Abascal's rent by 275% to €2,650 a month after acquiring the building; that figure is the union's account reported by AFP.
Spain's official statistics agency reported that national home-sale prices were 12.9% higher year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026; the Madrid region's increase was 13.5%.

Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez characterized the eviction as a consequence of speculation, while Socialist congressional spokesperson Patxi López said Madrid's city and regional authorities were responsible for housing and that the owners had rejected purchase offers.

The initial spontaneous protest drew 10,000 people according to the central government's estimate, illustrating that turnout estimates and the scale of the reaction should be attributed rather than treated as a single settled count.

explore_lenses.label: What could change after the protests?
explore_lenses.title: Pressure is focused on tenant safeguards and public housing
explore_lenses.summary: Protesters are seeking stronger protections against eviction and lower housing costs, while the national government is pursuing a longer-term expansion of affordable public housing. Those programs may increase supply, but they do not by themselves resolve Abascal's immediate housing situation.

claims.text: Protest organizers said they would maintain the Puerta del Sol camp until housing is treated as a basic necessity rather than a market asset; this is an organizer's stated intention, not a confirmed duration.
Abascal said she hoped her case would help change laws that allowed her eviction; protesters have called for steps to curb costs and make evictions harder.

Spain's Council of Ministers approved the 2026-2030 State Housing Plan, allocating €7 billion over five years; at least 40% is earmarked for construction or acquisition of social and affordable homes.

The national government launched the CASA47 public-housing portal in September with 800 homes available and another 1,500 expected soon, but the homes are distributed nationwide rather than presented as a specific remedy for this case.

story_report.summary: The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, 87, from the Madrid home where she had lived for more than 70 years triggered mass demonstrations over Spain’s housing crisis. Tens of thousands joined protests calling for action to restrain housing costs and prevent evictions, while an initial spontaneous gathering drew an estimated 10,000 people, according to the central government. The case has become a focal point for competing accounts of responsibility, as national and Madrid authorities, the property owner and tenant advocates dispute how the removal could have been avoided.

sections.heading: Abascal Eviction and Legal Dispute
sections.body: Abascal was removed on September 23, 2026, during the fourth attempted eviction from her Retiro flat, where she had lived since 1956. The owner, Urbagestión Desarrollo e Inversión S.L., maintained that a second succession to the 1956 tenancy was invalid; Spain’s Supreme Court ruled for the owners in March 2026, reversing an earlier decision in her favor. A request from the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights for Spain to halt the eviction and ensure adequate housing did not stop the removal.

sections.heading: Housing Costs and Political Blame
sections.body: The Madrid Tenants’ Union said the building’s new owner raised Abascal’s rent by 275% to €2,650 a month, an account reported by AFP. Official figures show national home-sale prices rose 12.9% year on year in the first quarter of 2026, with a 13.5% increase in the Madrid region. Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez described the eviction as a result of speculation, while Socialist spokesperson Patxi López said Madrid’s city and regional authorities were responsible for housing and that the owners had rejected purchase offers.

sections.heading: Housing Measures and Continuing Protest
sections.body: Organizers said they would keep a camp at Puerta del Sol until housing is treated as a basic necessity rather than a market asset, though the duration remains an intention rather than a confirmed timetable. Abascal said she hoped her case would help change the laws that permitted her eviction. Separately, Spain approved a €7 billion, five-year state housing plan, with at least 40% assigned to social and affordable homes, and launched the CASA47 portal with 800 homes available and another 1,500 expected nationwide.

unresolved.text: Public reporting does not specify the terms of Madrid City Council’s housing offers or why they did not result in a settled alternative for Abascal before the eviction.

It remains unclear whether the demonstrations will produce changes to eviction rules, whether Madrid authorities will provide an acceptable alternative home for Abascal, and how quickly national housing-supply measures may affect rents.

related_stories.title: Pope Leo XIV Denounces Assisted Dying as 'False Compassion' in Lourdes Address
related_stories.summary: During his address at Lourdes, Pope Leo XIV condemned assisted dying, labeling it as 'false compassion'. He urged believers to reject the idea of causing death under the guise of compassion. This statement comes in the context of recent legislation in France that established a right to assisted dying for certain adults with incurable conditions.
